title: Tentmakers (Acts 18)
hookLine: Priscilla and Aquila work with Paul and teach Apollos more perfectly

cards: Picture a workshop in Corinth, a busy port city. Leather and canvas, needles, awls, the smell of hides. Three people bent over their work, talking while they stitch.
One of them is the Apostle Paul. It's easy to picture Paul only preaching to crowds or writing letters, and he did both. But much of his week, he was working with his hands to pay his own way.
Luke tells us exactly what the job was: they were tentmakers.

teach.b: The other two are a married couple, Aquila and Priscilla, Jews who had recently come from Rome, because the emperor Claudius had ordered Jews to leave the city.
Paul stays with them, the text says, because they shared his trade. He works with them through the week, and on the Sabbath he speaks in the synagogue.
The Greek word is skenopoioi, tent makers, though it may have meant leatherworkers more broadly.
In a letter probably written from Corinth, Paul reminds the Thessalonians that he worked night and day so as not to be a burden to anyone. Now jump ahead.

Priscilla and Aquila move with Paul to Ephesus, and a man named Apollos arrives from Alexandria: eloquent, mighty in the scriptures, on fire, teaching accurately about Jesus. But he knows only the baptism of John.
So what do Priscilla and Aquila do? They don't correct him in front of everyone.
In the Douay-Rheims, they "took him to them, and expounded to him the way of the Lord more diligently."
The Greek means more exactly; older English Bibles put it as more perfectly, today's line. They take him aside, probably to their home, maybe their workshop, and fill in what he's missing.
Then they send him on with letters of recommendation, and Apollos becomes a great help to the believers in Achaia. One more thing: more than once, Luke names Priscilla first.
Many scholars think that means she was the better known of the two, maybe the leading teacher. Two tentmakers quietly shaped a preacher Paul later names in the same breath as himself and Peter.

how: Catholics honor Saints Aquila and Priscilla, traditionally on July 8, and the Church teaches the dignity of ordinary work; many lay Catholics serve as catechists alongside their jobs.

games.q: you're Priscilla. a gifted new preacher in town is missing something important. what do you do?
o: stand up and correct him during his talk.
take him aside and explain more.
warn others not to listen to him.
games.why: she and Aquila take him aside, explain the way of God more perfectly, and then send him on with letters of welcome.

practice: Think of someone who is good at something, enthusiastic, maybe a little ahead of what they know: a new coworker, a younger relative, a friend who's just discovered something.

Picture doing what Priscilla and Aquila did: not correcting them in public, but taking them aside, adding what you know, and cheering them on. Then think of who once did that for you, and if you pray, give thanks for them.
